title: What is the cause? time? nature? necessity? chance? (1.1–1.2)
hook: the Shvetashvatara Upanishad opens like a seminar: a circle of thinkers lists every possible cause of the world, and none of them is enough

segments.voice: Yesterday: the rivers lose their names in the sea, astam, and the Mundaka came to a close. Your line was nama-rupa gone. Did you meet someone without their label first? Today, a new Upanishad, and a new week. Day four hundred twenty-one.

Why did things turn out this way? People ask it after a near miss on the highway, after a diagnosis, after meeting someone on a train they almost didn't catch. People reach for answers. It was just timing. That's how I am. It was meant to be. Pure luck. The Shvetashvatara Upanishad opens with a group of thinkers asking the same thing about the whole world, and it lines up the very same answers. Time. Nature. Fate. Chance. And then it does something brave. It says, none of these is enough.
screen: `WHY DID THINGS TURN OUT THIS WAY?` → `TIMING. NATURE. FATE. LUCK.` → `NONE OF THESE IS ENOUGH.`

segments.voice: It opens with the brahmavadins, people who talk about Brahman, in discussion. What is the cause? Is it Brahman? From where are we born? By what do we live? On what do we rest? Who governs us, as we move through pleasure and pain? Then the list of candidates. Kala, time: everything ripens and rots on its own schedule. Svabhava, inborn nature: fire is hot because that's what fire is. Niyati, necessity, fixed law, fate. Yadriccha, chance, whatever happens. The elements. The womb. The person, purusha. Should we think one of these is the cause? Some scholars link these to schools of thought in ancient India, and the text takes each one seriously. Then it gives its verdict. Not any one of them. Not even all of them combined, because there's a self here too. And the self, on its own, isn't master of its pleasure and pain either. So the seekers do something other than argue. They turn to meditation and yoga, and in meditation they see the power of God, hidden by its own qualities, the one who rules over all those causes, from time to the self. This Upanishad speaks of God as a person, the Lord, and later names him Rudra; Shaiva traditions hold it dear. A few verses on comes your line: the wheel of Brahman, vast, in which everything lives and rests. Tomorrow, the wheel itself.
screen: `WHAT IS THE CAUSE? WHO GOVERNS US?` · `TIME, NATURE, FATE, CHANCE.` · `NONE ALONE; NOT EVEN ALL COMBINED.` · `IN MEDITATION, THE POWER OF GOD.` · then, large: `BRAHMACHAKRA.`

segments.voice: Two minutes with the question of causes. Sit, and bring to mind one thing in your life you've wondered about: why it happened, why this way. Notice which answer you usually reach for. Just timing? Just how I am? Meant to be? Pure luck? Hold that answer loosely. Then, like the seekers, stop arguing with it. Let the question sit in the quiet, and just breathe beside it, without needing to settle it today. The bell holds the time.
Brahmacakra, the wheel of Brahman. The Shvetashvatara opens by asking what is the cause, time, nature, necessity, chance, and finds no single answer enough, until the seekers turn to meditation.

Your line: the wheel of Brahman. Today, when you catch yourself saying it's just luck or it's just how I am, pause and ask the Upanishad's question: is that really enough? Day four hundred twenty-one.

howItsDone: The Shvetashvatara is studied across Vedanta schools and has a special place in Shaiva traditions, which honor its praise of Rudra-Shiva as the Lord who rules over time and all other causes.

fork.setup: you're in the circle of seekers. time, nature, fate, chance: none of them explains the world. what do you do?
options: pick the likeliest and move on.
turn to meditation and yoga, and look.
decide the question has no answer.
fork.reveal: they practice dhyana-yoga, and see the power of God, hidden in its own qualities, who rules every cause from time to the self.

original.note: Sanskrit brahmacakra, the wheel of Brahman: the vast wheel of Shvetashvatara 1.6, in which all things live and rest.

trapdoor: what you thought: it's either fate or luck.
what it means: the Shvetashvatara weighs time, nature, fate, chance, the elements, the womb and the person, and finds none enough alone.
what a scholar hears: kālaḥ svabhāvo niyatir yadṛcchā bhūtāni yoniḥ puruṣa iti cintyā (1.2): a list some scholars read as echoing positions held by schools of the time.

notes: 1.1–1.3 paraphrased from memory; 1.2 list (kala, svabhava, niyati, yadrccha, bhutani, yoni, purusha) and 'not their combination, because of the self; the self too is not master (anisha) of pleasure and pain'. Confirm.

'Thinkers in ancient India really did hold views like these' (e.g. kalavada, svabhavavada, niyati of the Ajivikas): now softened to 'many scholars link these' in the teach and trapdoor; the match of each term to a specific school is debated. Confirm.
Rudra is named in chapter 3 (3.2 and following); confirm 'later names him Rudra'.
Shaiva traditions' regard for the Shvetashvatara: general; confirm.
